Saudi Arabia is quietly becoming the gaming industry's biggest player... 😶

text:

In Dubai's tokenisation pilot, the only per-investor cap I found is in the platform's terms, not the rulebook.

text:
QatarEnergy's recent $800 million contract with China's COOEC to install over 100 km of subsea infrastructure at the Maydan Mahzam field marks a significant step in modernizing a mature offshore asset that has been producing since 1965. This 66-month project encompasses pipelines, power cables, and umbilicals installation, critical for maintaining and extending the field's operational life amid declining global oil reserves. 

The Maydan Mahzam upgrade underscores the industry's shift towards sustaining production from aging fields while balancing exploration efforts. This approach resonates with trends seen in major discoveries of the 21st century, where early-stage results and reservoir quality have driven long-term value rather than immediate production spikes. 

Moreover, the contract highlights the complexity and technical demands of subsea engineering, a domain where event-driven catalysts like contract awards and installation milestones significantly influence market perception. Similar to recent developments from ReconAfrica, where exploration updates have shaped investor sentiment, QatarEnergy's phased execution and engineering progress will be key near-term catalysts to watch.

This project exemplifies the upstream focus on asset integrity and basin validation over short-term financial engineering, aligning with the technical mindset of industry insiders and operators.

This was at the heart of the roundtable I had the opportunity to moderate at Everest Group  Engage Bengaluru 2026, where fifteen industry leaders came together to reassess the boundaries of GCC and outsourced work.

Three key takeaways stood out for me:

▪ 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗚𝗖𝗖 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘂𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴. The real decision is which capabilities an enterprise should own and build, and where partners can bring greater expertise, scale and flexibility.

author: George Mraovic
headline: Strategic Capital Positioning Across KSA, MENA, EU & US/LATAM | Founder - Blackwave Capital
text:
The most valuable information in an investor meeting is sometimes the reason they won't invest.

A conversation with an institutional investor in the Middle East today reinforced something that founders frequently underestimate: capital is not allocated against opportunity alone. It is allocated against a specific set of risks an investor is willing to underwrite.

A company may have a compelling product, a significant addressable market and strong alignment with regional economic priorities, yet remain outside a fund's current investment parameters.

The distinction is important.

An early-stage investor may underwrite product risk but not regulatory uncertainty. A growth investor may accept international expansion risk but require proven commercial economics. A strategic investor may prioritize regional integration over near-term financial returns.

The same business can therefore represent three entirely different investment propositions.

This is particularly relevant when navigating capital markets across Saudi Arabia, the UAE and the broader MENA region, where understanding the differences between institutional venture capital, family offices and strategic capital is essential.

Effective fundraising requires understanding not only where capital is available, but also:

• Which risks investors are prepared to absorb.

• Which commercial milestones change the investment decision.

• Whether new capital will accelerate a proven business model or finance its validation.

The question is whether private capital joins before the final close.

text:
Signs of a mature market: a Japanese bank lending in riyals against a Saudi BNPL loan book - and using a shariah compliant structure! 

MUFG has provided Tamara, the Kingdom's first homegrown fintech unicorn, with SAR 749 million in riyal funding through a securitisation facility. According to Tamara, no international bank has done this for a fintech in the region before.

That says a lot about how far the Saudi financial market has come, and the growing confidence of international institutions in its fintech ecosystem.

I have worked with Japanese Banks during my project finance days on regional greenfield petrochemical and power/water projects and it’s encouraging to see them expanding to new areas - a testimony to the longstanding strategic and commercial ties between Asia and the GCC.

And it shows securitisation is starting to work here. That gives fintechs, lenders and eventually SMEs another way to fund growth beyond the traditional bank loan.

Very positive news for Saudi and the region.
